unit.title: Coordinate the installation of electrical cable and fixture

summary: This unit teaches you to coordinate the cabling and fixtures stage of an electrical installation: reading cable and luminaire schedules, ordering and controlling materials, handling drums and pulling cables without damage, terminating neatly, choosing and fixing lighting and other fixtures for the place and the climate, setting up controls and emergency lighting, and supervising the crew through testing, snagging and handover.

blocks.p: Once the supports, conduit and boxes are in, the **cable and fixture stage** turns a building site into a working installation. Cables are ordered, delivered, drawn in, labelled and terminated; light fittings, fans, heaters, sensors and emergency lights are fixed and connected; the circuits are tested, snags are cleared and the client is shown how everything works. At Level 3 you coordinate this stage. You plan it from the schedules and drawings, control the materials, brief and supervise the crew, agree the work with other trades, check quality, and prepare the handover. (The supports that carry the cables are covered in MEMMRD0673A, and testing procedures in MEMMRD0663A.)

blocks.h: What you must be able to do

head: Task
What it looks like on the job
rows: Use the cable schedule and luminaire schedule to plan quantities, the order of the pulls and what each area needs.
Choose drum lengths, check deliveries, store cable and fittings safely, guard against theft, record issues and returns.
Plan the pull, set up the drum, respect pulling tension and bending radius, communicate, label and check for damage.
Fix cables so they are supported, and make neat, tight, correct terminations.
Match fittings to the schedule, the place, the climate and the ceiling or wall they go into; use correct ratings and lamps.
Fix lights, fans, heaters, sensors and isolators firmly, with the protective conductor connected, and in the right order with other trades.
Set up controls and emergency lighting
Connect dimmers, photocells, sensors and emergency fittings correctly, including the permanent charging supply.
Agree layouts, order of work and protection of finished fittings with ceiling, painting and other crews.
Set the standard, check early and often, control hazards, and deal with defective work.
Arrange dead tests, function tests by a competent person, a snag list, documents and a client briefing.

ul: Supply is **110/220 V, 50 Hz**. Lighting and outlets are usually 110 V; heavier loads such as water heaters and air-conditioners are 220 V.

The code used is based on the US **National Electrical Code (NEC)**. Cable sizes are often given in **AWG** (American wire gauge) as well as in mm². Designers may use British terms. This kit gives both: **luminaire** is the British word for a light fitting, and **fixture** the American one.
Heat, humidity, salt air, strong sun, heavy rain and hurricanes affect which cables and fittings last. Termites and rats attack cables in roof spaces.
**Copper cable theft** from building sites is a real problem. Security of materials is part of your job.

blocks.note: Where the specification and your habit differ, follow the specification. Where the specification and a maker's instructions differ, raise it with the designer before you fix anything.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: You do not only do the work: you plan it, order the materials, brief the crew, check the quality, report progress and take responsibility for safety and for the handover. Read the sections in order; they follow the job from schedules to handover.
A **cable schedule** lists every cable on the project: its **reference**, **size and type**, **route**, **length** and the **two ends** it connects. Use it to:

ul: work out how much of each cable to order, and the drum lengths;
plan the order of the pulls and give the crew each day's cables;
tick off each cable as it is pulled, labelled and terminated, and record the **actual length** used;
show progress honestly: done, left to do, problems;
record changes, with the date and who agreed them, so the final schedule matches what was installed.

blocks.p: A **luminaire (fixture) schedule** lists each type of fitting: its reference, make or specification, lamp or LED details, colour temperature, mounting, IP rating, control and where it is used, with the quantity. Use it to order the right numbers, check deliveries against it, issue fittings to each area, and mark off each fitting as it is installed and tested.

The route length measured on the drawing is not the length of cable you need. Add an allowance for **drops** to switches and outlets, **terminations** at the boards and fittings, slack for tidy connections, and waste: commonly **10 to 15%**, as the project or company states. **Example:** a route of 52 m with a 15% allowance needs 52 × 1.15 = 59.8 m, so cut about 60 m.

Cable is sold on drums or in coils of set lengths. Choose lengths so that each run is **one piece**, with no joint along it. Joints are weak points and must be made in a suitable, accessible enclosure. **Example:** two runs of 88 m and 61 m, each with a 15% allowance, need 101 m and 70 m, which is 171 m in all. One 250 m drum gives both runs with 79 m left over for the next job; two 100 m drums would not give the 101 m run in one piece. Work out the cutting plan on paper before ordering, and keep the leftover lengths on record.

head: Item
What to do
rows: Check type, size, quantity, length and condition against the order and the schedule. Write damage or shortage on the delivery note **before** you sign, and report it to the supplier.
Store on firm, level ground or in a store, with the cable ends **sealed** to keep out moisture and dirt. Roll a drum only in the direction of the arrow painted on it.
Keep in their boxes in a dry, locked store, off the floor and away from other trades' work, so they are not damaged or covered in dust.
Record everything in, everything issued to each area and everything returned, so losses show up quickly.
Have copper delivered close to when it is needed. Lock cable and fittings in a store. Do not leave drums or offcuts lying about, and control the store key.
At the end of the job, return unused cable and fittings to stores and record them. Recycle scrap through the company's proper route, never by burning insulation or selling privately.

flow: First fix: boxes, conduit, trunking and supports built in before plastering and ceilings
Cables drawn in and labelled; ends protected
Plastering, ceilings and painting by the other trades
Second fix: fit and connect accessories, luminaires, fans and controls
Dead tests; function tests by a competent person
Snagging, documents and handover

blocks.p: Fixtures and accessories are normally fitted **after plastering and painting**, so they are not damaged or covered in plaster. Agree the order with the other trades and protect finished work.

blocks.h: Planning the crew and sharing equipment

ul: When two crews need the same scaffold, MEWP or tools, plan the order and give each crew set times.
Give each member a clear task and area. Brief the crew at the start of each day on the work, materials, access equipment and hazards.
Match tasks to skill; pair newer workers with experienced ones.

head: Task
Method
Example
rows: 50 fittings at J$3 800 = J$190 000 (GCT is added at the current rate)

sections.title: Handling cable and pulling it in

head: Need
Cable choice
rows: PVC-insulated copper conductors in conduit or trunking, or sheathed cable, of the size the design gives
Circuits that must work for a time in a fire (emergency lighting, fire alarm)
Fire-resistant cable, kept apart from other cables
UV-resistant sheath, or cable in UV-resistant conduit
Cable made for it, with sealed glands
Hot places (near lamps, in roof spaces)
Insulation rated for the temperature; heat-resistant flex for pendants with hot lamps
A ferrule (or a lug) on the end, so the strands cannot spread or be cut by the screw

ul: Roll a drum a short distance only in the direction of the **arrow** on its flange, so the cable does not loosen and unwind. Never drop it from a truck or drag it.
Lift with a forklift, hoist or ramp, not by hand: a full drum can weigh hundreds of kilograms.
Seal a cut end with a cap or tape so moisture and dirt do not enter.
Pay out from a drum mounted on a **spindle and stands**, so it turns freely under control. Never lay it flat to pull from the top, and never stand it unsupported on its edge.

flow: Read the cable schedule and the maker's data: pulling tension and minimum bending radius
Walk the route: tray, conduit and boxes finished, clean, with no sharp edges
Decide where the drum, rollers and corner sheaves go
Choose the method: by hand, rope, fish tape or winch
Give roles: one person in charge, a drum handler, feeders and pullers
Agree radios or signals, with a clear stop signal that anyone may use
Brief the crew on hazards; barrier the area
Pull; label; seal; check for damage; record the length

blocks.p: Cables must not be pulled harder than the maker allows, or the conductors stretch and thin. A common figure when pulling on the conductors (with a pulling eye) is about **70 N per mm² of copper conductor**: the **maximum pulling tension** is the number of conductors × their area × 70. **Example:** a 4-core cable with 16 mm² conductors: 4 × 16 × 70 = 4 480 N. Pulling with a stocking grip on the sheath allows much less, so use the maker's figure for the grip you have. Use a **winch with a tension meter or a weak link** on long or heavy pulls, so the limit cannot be passed.

head: Problem during a pull
Likely cause
What to do
rows: A jam, a tight bend, a missing roller, a joint snagging
Stop. Find the cause and clear it. Never just pull harder.
Too many cables, rough conduit, no lubricant, too many bends
Stop; use cable lubricant, add a draw-in box, or check the fill.
Sheath scraped through to the insulation
Stop. Assess the damage and replace or repair as the specification allows. Never cover with tape and carry on.
Bent too tightly, or a roller out of place

blocks.p: Every cable has a **minimum bending radius**, usually a multiple of its overall diameter: often about **6 to 12 times** for power cables, more for large single cores. **Example:** a 28 mm cable with a 12 × rule needs a radius of at least 12 × 28 = 336 mm. Use **cable rollers** along the route and a **corner sheave** at bends, so the cable is carried round the bend in an arc and never forced against a corner. A person's knee or a piece of timber is not a substitute.

head: Aid
Use
rows: Gets the pulling rope through conduit first
Grips the cable end so a rope or winch can pull it
Reduces friction in long conduit pulls; use a type that suits the cable sheath
Carry the cable and protect it at bends
Mechanical pull for long or heavy cables, with a tension limit
Keep the crew in contact; one person is in charge and anyone can call a stop

ul: **Label** each cable at both ends with its schedule reference, before it is terminated, so each end is matched to the schedule.
Leave enough length at each end for tidy terminations.
Seal the ends and protect them from damage and moisture.
Inspect the length for damage; record the actual length used and tick the cable off the schedule.

blocks.note: Cables laid on ceiling tiles must be lifted and supported on proper clips, tray or hangers. Tiles are not designed to carry cable.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.note: Pulling cables is a team job with pinch points at drums, rollers and ropes. Wear gloves, keep fingers clear, keep people out of the line of the rope, and make sure any worker can call 'Stop'.
blocks.label: Safety

flow: Strip the insulation to the length the terminal needs, without nicking the conductor
Fit a ferrule or lug to stranded conductors where required
Insert the conductor fully, with no bare copper showing outside the terminal
Tighten to the maker's torque, using a torque screwdriver where specified
Tug-test each conductor gently
Fold the conductors neatly into the box, so the plate fits with no strain on the terminals
Label and photograph where the specification asks

head: Fault
Why it matters
rows: Insulation stripped too far, bare copper showing
A risk of contact and short circuit
Strands cut off or left out of the terminal
Less current-carrying area; the joint overheats
A high-resistance joint heats up and can start a fire
Terminal too tight on a stranded conductor
Two conductors under one screw where the terminal is made for one

blocks.p: Use **crimpers** to fix lugs and ferrules: a crimp made with pliers is not reliable. Make joints only where the specification allows, in an accessible, suitable box, never buried in a ceiling or wall.

ul: Support cables on clips, tray, hangers or straps at the spacing the specification gives. Do not rest them on suspended ceiling tiles or the ceiling grid, and do not tie them to the ceiling's hangers.
Keep cables away from sharp edges, hot pipes and moving parts, and segregated from data and fire-alarm cables as specified.
Seal the glands and cable entries of outdoor boxes, with entries facing down where possible.
Show the crew the standard before work starts, with a sample installation of each type of fitting and termination.
Check the **first items** each person does, and correct faults at once, explaining why.
Follow with regular spot checks, more often for work that had faults.
Keep a simple quality checklist for each area, signed when it passes, and a **snag list** for faults, with each corrected by the person who made it.

head: Term
Unit
Meaning
rows: Total light output of a lamp or fitting
Light falling on a surface: 1 lux = 1 lumen per square metre
How much light you get for each watt: LED lamps and fittings commonly give around 80 to 150 lm/W
How warm or cool the light looks: 2 700–3 000 K is warm white, about 4 000 K neutral, 5 000–6 500 K cool daylight
How naturally the light shows colours: 80 or more is usual for general work, 90 or more where colour matters

blocks.p: The design sets the lux level, from the code or standard for the use. As a rough guide, usual maintained levels are about **100 lux** in corridors, **150 to 200 lux** in restaurants and lounges, **300 lux** in classrooms and general offices, **500 lux** for detailed desk work and kitchens. Follow the design figure.

blocks.h: How many fittings? The lumen method

blocks.p: **Number of fittings = (lux × room area) ÷ (lumens per fitting × utilisation factor × maintenance factor).** The **utilisation factor** (about 0.4 to 0.7) allows for light lost to walls and ceiling; the **maintenance factor** (about 0.8) allows for dirt and ageing. **Example:** a classroom 9 m × 6 m (54 m²) needs 300 lux. Each fitting gives 3 600 lm; utilisation 0.5; maintenance 0.8. Number = (300 × 54) ÷ (3 600 × 0.5 × 0.8) = 16 200 ÷ 1 440 = 11.25, so fit **12**, arranged evenly. Measure the result with a **lux meter** at desk height after installation.

head: Type
Used for
Points to check
rows: Fixed to solid support; suited to the ceiling type
Cut-out size agreed with the ceiling installer; rated for contact with insulation or kept clear; driver accessible
Weight and the fixing point; heat-resistant flex where lamps run hot
Fan-rated box or bracket fixed to the structure; blade height; balanced blades
IP rating, UV-resistant, corrosion resistance, fixing and wind load
Linear LED strip (often 12 V or 24 V DC)
Needs a matching low-voltage driver; never connect it direct to 110/220 V
Battery type and duration; charging supply

ul: An LED fitting has a **driver** that turns mains into the low-voltage DC the LEDs need. Keep the driver accessible and ventilated; heat shortens its life. If a fitting flickers, a new driver or a loose connection is often the cause.

Use a **dimmer listed for the LED load and for the dimming method** (leading edge or trailing edge) the drivers use. Check the dimmer's **minimum and maximum load**: LED loads are small, so a dimmer rated for 400 W of filament lamps may not work properly below a minimum load, and may be overloaded if the total of the LEDs exceeds its LED rating.
**Example:** 30 fittings of 9 W each total 270 W. A dimmer rated for 20 to 150 W of LED load is overloaded. Use two dimmers, or one with a higher rating.

blocks.p: A recessed fitting covered by thermal insulation can overheat and start a fire, shortening the life of the LED and driver. Use fittings rated for contact with insulation, or keep the insulation clear by the distance the maker states.

head: Item
Fixing
rows: Light fitting on a suspended ceiling
Heavy or large fittings have their own hangers fixed to the structure. A fitting rests on the ceiling grid only as the maker allows, with extra hangers.
A fan-rated box or bracket fixed to a beam or a brace between joists. A fan's weight and shaking can pull an ordinary light box out.
First check its weight and that the fixing point can hold it, with a margin. Fix to the structure, not to ceiling board.
Stainless or galvanised fixings, sealed cable entry, gasket in good order, bracket and pole rated for the wind load
Mounted in boxes at the heights in the specification and drawings, level, with no strain on the terminals

ul: Always **isolate** the circuit first: switch off, lock off, tag, prove the tester, prove dead, prove the tester again.

Connect the **protective conductor** to the earth terminal of a Class I fitting, or through a connector. Never cut it short, join it to the neutral or leave it loose and bare. A Class II (double insulated) fitting has no earth connection; do not add one.
Connect line to the switch or control, never the neutral. The line goes to the centre contact of a screw lampholder.
Use **heat-resistant flex** for pendant fittings with hot lamps, and the correct size and type of flex for the load.
Use the maker's connectors and fold conductors neatly into the box so the cover fits without strain.

blocks.p: For a **220 V water heater** or similar fixed appliance, fit a **double-pole isolator within reach and in sight** of the appliance, and connect through it with cable of the size the design gives. Mark the isolator. An isolator out of sight, behind a cover or in another room, is not a safe isolation point.

head: Place
Requirements
rows: Fittings with an IP rating suited to rain and splashing; UV-resistant plastics; sealed cable entries, facing down; GFCI/RCD protection on the circuit

Fittings of the type and IP rating allowed for the zone; GFCI/RCD protection; no accessories within reach of the bath or shower; extra-low-voltage supply where the design requires it; fans and lights suited to the wet zone
Marine-grade finishes, stainless fixings and sealed glands
Fixing and structure rated for hurricane wind loads

ul: Compare the lighting layout with the ceiling grid, air-conditioning diffusers, sprinkler heads and smoke detectors, and agree a combined plan.
Make sure all cables, boxes and supports are in place before the ceiling closes, with drops in the right place and long enough.
Agree with the ceiling installer who cuts the holes and to what size, from the maker's data.
Fit luminaires after the tiles and the dusty work, and **cover them** if painting continues. Take lamps and diffusers out of harm's way, not off the fitting.
Leave access panels where junction boxes and drivers must be reached later.

head: Control
How it works
Points to check
rows: Right dimmer for the LEDs; switch in the line conductor
Switches an outdoor light on at dusk and off at dawn
Positioned so it does not see the fitting's own light, or it will switch on and off all night ('hunting'); placed away from other lights and shade
Correct time and programme; battery back-up as the maker says
Switches on when it detects movement
Position, range, time delay and sensitivity; keep it clear of heat sources and air-conditioning draughts
Set up and tested with the client

blocks.p: **Emergency lighting** lets people find their way out safely if the normal lighting fails in a power cut or a fire. It is shown on the design drawings: place fittings over exit doors, along escape routes, at changes of direction and level, at stairs, and near fire-fighting equipment and first-aid points.

head: Type
How it works
rows: Has its own battery and charger; normally fed from the local lighting circuit, so it lights when that circuit fails
The lamp is lit all the time, and stays on from the battery when the supply fails; common for exit signs in rooms used at night
The lamp is off normally and lights only when the supply fails
A central battery supplies slave fittings through fire-resistant cable

ul: A self-contained fitting needs a **permanent (unswitched) supply to charge its battery**, and, for maintained types, a switched supply as well. If the permanent supply is taken from the **switched** line by mistake, the battery goes flat each time the light is switched off.
The charging indicator is usually a green LED: if it is off after the supply has been restored, the battery is not charging; check the permanent supply, the fuse and the connections.

The design sets the **duration** the fittings must stay on (commonly 1 hour, or 3 hours for some premises) and the minimum light level on escape routes (a typical minimum is about 1 lux along the centre line of the escape route). Follow the code the design uses.

Use **fire-resistant cable**, where the design calls for it, so the circuit works for a time in a fire, and keep it **separate** from other cables so a fault or fire in an ordinary circuit does not damage it.

blocks.p: After installation, a **competent person** cuts the normal supply to each fitting (a test key or the circuit breaker) and checks that it lights and stays on for its rated time. The result is recorded in a **log book** kept by the client. The client is shown how to do the regular short function test (commonly monthly) and the full-duration test (commonly yearly), and to record each one.

blocks.h: Hazards on a cable and fixture job

head: Hazard
Controls
rows: Manual handling of drums, cable and fittings
Drum stands, trolleys and winches; team lifts; keep loads within safe weights
Pinch points at drums, rollers and ropes
Gloves, hands clear, one person in charge, a stop signal anyone can call
Mobile scaffold or platform steps, never chairs or boxes; barrier off and keep the area below clear
Electric shock when connecting to existing circuits
Safe isolation with a tester proved before and after
Dust, cuts and flying debris from cutting and drilling
Eye protection, masks, gloves; ream and deburr ends
Handle with care; dispose of broken lamps safely
Breaks in the shade, drinking water, lighter tasks at the hottest hours
Good housekeeping; cables and rope kept clear

flow: Inspect every area against the drawings and schedules: items present, right type, level, firmly fixed, clean, labelled
Dead tests with the circuits isolated: protective conductor continuity, insulation resistance (with lamps, drivers and electronics disconnected) and polarity
Record results and compare with expected values
A competent person follows the procedure to energise the circuits
Function tests: every switch, dimmer, sensor, photocell and emergency light works as designed
Snag, correct and recheck

blocks.p: Only a **competent person** energises new circuits for the function test, following the procedure. The newest trainee, the client or whoever is nearest the board does not.

A **snag list** is a list of defects and unfinished items to correct: for example fittings not level, a missing label, a loose plate. For each snag, record where it is, what is wrong, who will fix it and by when. The person who made the fault should correct it where possible, so they learn. Tick each off and recheck it.

ul: The certificate and test results.
The updated cable and luminaire schedules and **as-built drawings**.
The makers' instructions and **warranties** for the fixtures and controls.
The emergency lighting log book and test results.
Spare lamps, keys and any special tools, listed on the handover sheet.

blocks.p: Do not give the client the crew's timesheets, the supplier's invoices with your prices or your own phone bill: they are not part of the handover.

Walk round with the client. Show how the controls, dimmers, timers and sensors work, how to test the emergency lighting and the RCD test button, where the circuit chart is, and what maintenance is needed. Get their signature on the handover sheet.
Report to the supervisor, usually weekly, **against the schedules**: what is done, what is left to do and what problems there are, with photographs. Do not guess a percentage from memory.
Tick each statement only when you can do it without looking at the notes.

ul: I can use a cable schedule and a luminaire schedule to plan, order, issue and track the work.
I can work out cable lengths with an allowance and choose drum lengths.
I can receive, store and guard cable and fittings, and keep a stores record.
I can describe the order of work from first fix to handover.
I can handle and set up a drum correctly.
I can plan a pull, assign roles and agree signals.
I can work out a maximum pulling tension and a minimum bending radius from the maker's data.
I can use rollers, sheaves, lubricant and a winch correctly, and deal with a problem during a pull.
I can label, seal, check and record each cable after the pull.
I can make neat, correct terminations and list the faults that go wrong.
I can support cables properly and keep them away from ceiling tiles.
I can use lumens, lux, CCT and efficacy, and work out how many fittings a room needs.
I can choose a dimmer for an LED load and check its rating.
I can fix heavy fittings and fans to the structure and connect the protective conductor correctly.
I can install a fixed appliance with a local isolator.
I can choose fittings for wet and outdoor places, and for the Jamaican climate.
I can agree layouts and the order of work with the ceiling installer and other trades.
I can connect a photocell, time switch or sensor sensibly.
I can explain how emergency lighting is installed, supplied, tested and recorded.
I can control the hazards of the job and supervise quality.
I can arrange dead tests, function tests, a snag list, documents and a client briefing.

head: Figure
What it is
rows: Usual allowance added to the drawn cable length
About 70 N per mm² of copper
Typical maximum pulling tension on the conductors (follow the maker)
Typical minimum bending radius of power cable (follow the maker)
The lumen method for the number of fittings
A typical minimum along the centre line of an escape route
Common emergency lighting durations (follow the design)

terms: The smallest radius a cable may be bent to without damage.
The list of each cable's reference, size, type, route, length and ends.
How warm or cool a light looks, in kelvin.
A roller set that carries a cable round a corner during a pull.
The unit that turns mains into the low-voltage DC an LED needs.
A small metal sleeve crimped on the end of a stranded conductor.
The light falling on a surface, in lumens per square metre.
Ingress protection: protection against solids and water.
The unit of the total light output of a lamp.
An emergency fitting lit all the time, and on from its battery when the supply fails.
The greatest force with which the maker allows a cable to be pulled.
An emergency fitting that lights only when the supply fails.
A light sensor that switches an outdoor light on at night.
A passive infrared sensor that detects movement.
Fitting and connecting accessories and fittings after plastering and painting.
A list of defects and unfinished items to correct.
The share of a lamp's light that reaches the working surface.

c1.title: A riser pull in a Montego Bay hotel
c1.text: Dwayne leads a crew pulling a 4-core, 16 mm² copper cable, 95 m long, from the ground-floor board to the sixth floor of a hotel in Montego Bay, through tray and a vertical riser with two 90° bends. The cable maker allows a pulling tension of 70 N per mm² of conductor when pulled by a pulling eye on the conductors, and a minimum bending radius of 12 times the overall diameter, which is 28 mm. The crew use a winch with a tension meter, and radios. On the walk-through, Dwayne finds a sharp burr at one tray joint.

c2.title: Lighting a restaurant in Ocho Rios
c2.text: Shauna coordinates the lighting for a new restaurant dining room, 8 m × 6 m, in Ocho Rios, St Ann. The design asks for 200 lux, with warm, welcoming light, on dimmers. Each LED downlight gives 800 lm; the design uses a utilisation factor of 0.5 and a maintenance factor of 0.8. Each downlight uses 9 W. The owner wants all of them on one dimmer. The electrical supplier offers a dimmer listed for LED loads of 20 to 150 W.

c3.title: Path lights at a Treasure Beach guest house
c3.text: Kimani's crew is fitting twelve outdoor path lights along a garden path at a guest house at Treasure Beach, St Elizabeth, about 40 m from the sea. The lights switch on at night through one photocell. On the first night test, the lights switch on and off repeatedly through the evening. The supplier's brochure shows fittings in IP20, IP44 and IP65. The cable entries on the fittings face upwards, and the circuit is fed from an indoor breaker with no RCD.

c4.title: Emergency lighting in a Half Way Tree school hall
c4.text: A school hall in Half Way Tree, St Andrew, used for evening concerts, is being fitted with self-contained emergency luminaires and exit signs, to be installed by Tashana's crew. The design asks for maintained exit signs over the doors and non-maintained fittings along the aisles, each with a 3-hour battery. The crew find that the charging supply for the luminaires has been taken from the switched line of the hall lighting circuit. After the supply was restored following one test, a luminaire's green charging indicator stayed off.

c5.title: Ordering cable for a Black River clinic wing
c5.text: A new clinic wing in Black River, St Elizabeth, has 18 rooms. The cable schedule shows 40 m of lighting and outlet cable per room, measured on the drawing, and the company adds 15% for drops, terminations and waste. Cable costs J$310 per metre. It is sold on 100 m and 250 m drums. Each room has 2 light fittings at J$3 200 each. The company's stores record every issue, and copper theft has been a problem on nearby sites.

questions.q: What is the most force the winch may put on the cable?
questions.why: Maximum pulling tension = conductors × area × 70 N/mm² = 4 × 16 × 70 = 4 480 N. Pulling on only one conductor (1 120 N) would be too cautious, and a figure above the limit would stretch and thin the conductors. A tension meter or weak link keeps the pull below the limit.

questions.q: What is the smallest radius at which the cable may be bent in the riser?
o: About 168 mm
About 28 mm
About 2 800 mm
About 336 mm
questions.why: Minimum bending radius = 12 × overall diameter = 12 × 28 = 336 mm. A tighter bend can damage the cable's insulation and conductors, so the tray and conduit bends, and the corner sheaves, must give at least this radius.

questions.q: What should Dwayne do about the sharp burr at the tray joint before the pull?
o: Pull slowly past it and check the sheath afterwards
Have it removed or covered before the cable passes
Place a roller beside it and pull as before
Leave it and use more lubricant at that point
questions.why: A sharp edge can cut the sheath and insulation as the cable is dragged across it. Remove or file smooth the burr, or cover it with a suitable guard, before the pull. A roller or lubricant does not make a sharp edge safe.

questions.q: Midway through the pull, the tension meter climbs towards the limit. What should happen?
o: Stop, find the cause, and clear it before going on
Pull slightly harder, as the cable is already part way in
Add more people to the rope to share the pull
Run the winch faster to carry the cable through the bend
questions.why: A sharp rise in tension means a jam, a tight bend, a missing roller or a snag. Pulling harder, or faster, damages the cable. Anyone can call 'Stop'; the crew finds and clears the cause, then restarts.

questions.q: How many downlights does the dining room need by the lumen method?
questions.why: N = (lux × area) ÷ (lumens × UF × MF) = (200 × 48) ÷ (800 × 0.5 × 0.8) = 9 600 ÷ 320 = 30. Leaving out the maintenance factor gives 24, which would fall below 200 lux once the fittings are dirty or aged.

questions.q: The owner wants a warm, welcoming dining room. Which colour temperature should Shauna specify?
o: About 6 500 K, cool daylight
About 4 000 K, neutral white
About 10 000 K, a very cool white
About 2 700 to 3 000 K
questions.why: Warm white (2 700–3 000 K) gives the soft, yellowish light people expect in restaurants and lounges. Cool daylight tones (5 000–6 500 K) suit work areas. Colour temperature is given in kelvin on the luminaire schedule.

questions.q: The 30 downlights total 270 W on the dimmer listed for 20 to 150 W of LED load. What should Shauna do?
o: Use one dimmer anyway, since LEDs draw very little current
Remove half of the downlights and light the room less
Use a dimmer rated for filament lamps, with a lower minimum
Use two dimmers, or one rated for a higher load
questions.why: 270 W is above the dimmer's 150 W LED rating, so it would overheat or fail. Split the load over two dimmers (each 135 W) or choose a dimmer rated for at least 270 W of LED load, and check it suits the driver's dimming method.

questions.q: Why do the path lights switch on and off repeatedly?
o: The lamps are too bright for a photocell to work with
The circuit is overloaded, so its breaker keeps tripping
Its light makes the photocell switch the fittings off
The photocell works only when the weather is cloudy
questions.why: If the photocell can see the fitting's own light, it decides it is day, switches the lights off, sees darkness, and switches them on again, so they 'hunt'. Move or shield the photocell so it sees only natural light, and away from other lights.

questions.q: Which IP rating is the best choice for these path lights?
o: IP20
IP44
IP65
IP00
questions.why: Path lights outside get rain, spray and dust. IP65 is dust-tight and resists water jets, while IP20 only keeps fingers out and IP44 resists only splashing. The brochure's IP65 fitting is the suitable one, and it also suits a site near the sea if its finish is corrosion-resistant.

questions.q: The cable entries on the fittings face upwards. What is the best arrangement?
o: Leave them, as the sealing gland will keep out the water
Drill holes in the base so that any water drains out
Face the entries down and seal the glands properly
Cover the entries with tape to stop rain entering them
questions.why: With entries facing up, rain runs straight down the cable into the fitting. Entries facing down, with the glands tightened and sealed, shed water. Tape does not give a lasting seal in sun and rain.

questions.q: The path lights are fed from a circuit with no RCD. What should Kimani do?
o: Nothing: outdoor lights are low power, so no RCD is needed
Fit the RCD only if the lights are within reach of the guests
Arrange GFCI/RCD protection for the outdoor circuit
Fit a larger breaker, so that the circuit does not trip in rain
questions.why: Outdoor circuits are exposed to rain and to people standing on wet ground, so GFCI/RCD protection is needed. A larger breaker gives no protection against shock.

questions.q: Why are the exit signs over the doors maintained, but the aisle fittings non-maintained?
o: Exit signs must be visible whenever the hall is in use
Maintained fittings last longer than non-maintained ones
Non-maintained fittings give more light than maintained ones
Exit signs need no battery, because they are always lit
questions.why: People using the hall in the evening need to see the exit signs at all times, so those are lit all the time (maintained), and they stay on from the battery when the supply fails. The aisle fittings need only light in an emergency (non-maintained).

questions.q: What is wrong with taking the charging supply from the switched line of the lighting circuit?
o: The battery stops charging whenever the lights go off
The luminaire will work normally, but will use too much power
The fitting will light up only when the room lights are on
The circuit will trip as soon as the battery is fully charged
questions.why: A self-contained luminaire needs a permanent, unswitched supply to keep its battery charged. If the supply comes from the switched line, the battery goes flat each time the lights are off, and the fitting may not last its rated time in an emergency.

questions.q: A luminaire's green charging LED stays off after the supply is restored. What is the best first step?
o: Replace the luminaire, since a dead indicator means it has failed
Ignore it, because the indicator is only a decoration
Switch the circuit on and off several times until it lights
Check its permanent supply, fuse and connections, isolated
questions.why: The indicator shows that the battery is charging. If it stays off, the charger may not have a supply: a wrongly connected or blown permanent supply, a loose connection or a fuse. Check these with the circuit isolated, and record the finding.

questions.q: How much cable should be ordered for the clinic wing, with the 15% allowance?
questions.why: 18 rooms × 40 m = 720 m on the drawing; adding 15% gives 720 × 1.15 = 828 m. 720 m would be short once drops, terminations and waste are counted.

questions.q: What is the cost of 828 m of cable, before GCT?
questions.why: 828 × J$310 = J$256 680, before GCT, which is added at the current rate. The figure J$223 200 is the cost of 720 m, without the allowance.

questions.q: Which action best reduces the risk of copper theft on this site?
o: Paint the drums a bright colour so thieves will avoid them
Pull all the cable in on the first day, before it is needed
Time deliveries close to need and lock the cable away
Order everything at once to save on delivery costs
questions.why: Cable is most at risk when it sits on site. Order and deliver it close to the time of use, keep it locked in a store with a controlled key, and record every issue and return so a loss shows up quickly. Pulling everything in at once puts it in the building before it is needed and ties up the crew.

questions.q: A fixture gives 1 200 lm from 10 W of power. What is its luminous efficacy?
o: 120 lm/W
12 lm/W
questions.why: Efficacy = lumens ÷ watts = 1 200 ÷ 10 = 120 lm/W, a typical figure for a good LED fitting. A higher efficacy means more light for the same electricity.

questions.q: A 110 V lighting circuit may lose no more than 3% of its voltage in the cable. What is the largest voltage drop allowed?
questions.why: 3% of 110 V = 110 × 0.03 = 3.3 V. If the calculated or measured drop is more than this, use a larger cable or shorten the run.

questions.q: Two lengths of cable must be joined above a plasterboard ceiling. Which is the correct way?
o: Twist and tape the conductors, then lay them in the void
Solder the joint and cover it with plaster and paint
Place the joint in the wall, behind the switch plate
Avoid it, or make it in an accessible, suitable box
questions.why: Joints are weak points and must be made in a suitable enclosure that stays accessible for inspection and repair, with an access panel where needed. A better solution is to avoid joints by choosing drum lengths to give each run in one piece.
